chapterTitle: Data Warehousing and Lake Solutions with Redshift and S3
aiGenerationNote:
Create a 15-minute mixed-media lesson. Start with a slide deck explaining the difference between data warehouses and data lakes, highlighting Redshift and S3 roles. Then, transition to a live demo showing the creation of an S3 bucket, uploading a sample Parquet file, and configuring an AWS Glue Crawler in the console. Show the resulting table in the Glue Data Catalog. Next, demonstrate connecting Redshift Spectrum to this Glue table and running a cross-source SQL query (Redshift internal table + S3 external table). screens.title: Data Warehousing and Lake Solutions
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll explore two complementary pillars of analytics on AWS: a high-performance data warehouse using Amazon Redshift, and a scalable data lake built on Amazon S3. You will learn how Redshift uses columnar storage, compression, and massively parallel processing to run complex analytics, and how RA3 instances separate compute and managed storage so you can scale each independently. You'll also see how Redshift Spectrum queries open formats in S3 using the AWS Glue Data Catalog, making a lakehouse-style architecture possible. On the data lake side, we'll cover practical S3 design: logical organization, partitioning by common filters like year and month, and why those choices reduce query cost. Then we'll examine Glue as the metadata and ETL backbone, and Lake Formation as the centralized security layer for table, column, and row permissions. Through a short hands-on workflow you will configure a crawler, create an external schema, and write a cross-source S Q L join. By the end you will know when to keep data in place on S3 and query it from Redshift, and when to load curated data into Redshift. We'll emphasize common mistakes—like missing partitioning or ignoring distribution keys—and practical mitigations. Ready to begin designing a balanced, cost-effective analytics platform?

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Data Warehousing and Lake Solutions
Data Warehousing and Lake Solutions
Design analytics platforms that balance performance, cost, and governance using Redshift and S3.

In this chapter you'll compare warehouses and lakes, learn Redshift operational choices like RA3, distribution and sort keys, and implement a workflow connecting S3 data to Redshift via Spectrum and Glue.

In this lesson
Amazon Redshift
Columnar MPP warehouse; RA3 managed storage; query tuning.
S3 Data Lake
Raw storage, partitioning, low-cost long-term retention.
AWS Glue & Lake Formation
Metadata, crawlers, ETL, and centralized access control.
Redshift Spectrum
Query S3 data in place using Glue Data Catalog tables.
Visual concept
How the pieces connect
Data flow snapshot
Raw events land in S3. Glue crawlers register schemas. Redshift queries S3 via Spectrum or loads curated tables for fast BI.
Common optimization
Partition S3 data by filters like year/month, choose distribution keys in Redshift based on join patterns, and use RA3 to right-size compute.
Explore Key Topics
Redshift tuning
Distribution and sort keys, RA3 managed storage, and concurrency scaling reduce cost and speed queries.
S3 lake design
Logical folders and partitioning make queries efficient for Athena and Spectrum.
Metadata & security
Glue Catalog plus Lake Formation provide discoverability and fine-grained access control.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next fifteen minutes you'll gain concrete skills for designing and operating analytics platforms. First, you'll learn to design scalable and cost-effective Redshift warehouses: choose instance types, employ RA3 managed storage, and select distribution and sort keys based on query patterns. For example, when joins repeatedly use a customer_id, a KEY distribution can dramatically reduce data movement. Second, you'll implement advanced Redshift features like Concurrency Scaling and Spectrum so your cluster handles concurrent read bursts and queries S3 in place. We'll show how Spectrum leverages the Glue Data Catalog so you can query Parquet files without loading them. These objectives matter because analytics at petabyte scale needs predictable performance and cost control. You'll practice reasoning about compute versus storage, and how to avoid common mistakes like uniform sort keys for all queries. Each objective ties directly to a hands-on workflow: crawling S3 with Glue, creating an external schema in Redshift, and writing a cross-source S Q L join. By the end you will be able to choose when to keep data in S3 and when to load it into Redshift, and you'll know the tools for controlling access and metadata.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide ties the learning goals to a concrete workflow you'll practice. First, design: pick RA3 or other instance families and pick distribution or sort keys by analyzing query patterns and join columns. For example, a KEY distribution on user_id reduces data movement when joining large event and user tables. Second, operate: enable Concurrency Scaling to absorb spikes in ad-hoc BI queries and understand the daily credits model so you budget query bursts wisely. Third, integrate: build a data lake on S3 with partitioned Parquet files, use a Glue Crawler to populate the Data Catalog, and verify schema correctness before querying. Finally, secure and manage: register S3 with Lake Formation, grant table- or column-level SELECT permissions to roles, and avoid direct S3 access so queries go through the centralized enforcement layer. The hands-on task follows these steps: create a bucket, upload partitioned Parquet, run a crawler, create an external schema in Redshift, and write a S Q L join between Redshift and Spectrum tables. This maps objectives to repeatable steps and prepares you to design both an efficient pipeline and a secure governance model.

screens.title: When to use a Data Warehouse vs a Data Lake
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the practical difference between a data warehouse and a data lake is the foundation of good analytics architecture. A data warehouse like Redshift is optimized for structured, curated datasets and complex S Q L analytics. It uses columnar storage and MPP to accelerate aggregations and joins over large curated tables. A data lake on S3 is a flexible store for raw and semi-structured data at any scale; it's ideal for long-term retention, exploration, and machine learning. A simple rule of thumb: put long-term raw events, logs, and historical snapshots in the lake; keep curated, modeled tables that power dashboards in the warehouse. A concrete example: clickstream events arriving daily are best landed in S3 as partitioned Parquet files. Analysts can explore patterns in-place using Athena or Spectrum. When you need consistent, highly tuned reports that join sales and customer dimensions nightly, load those curated results into Redshift for fast BI queries. A common misconception is thinking one must always move everything into Redshift. That approach can be expensive and slow at petabyte scale. Instead, query S3 in place with Spectrum when possible, and load only the curated subsets that need warehouse performance. Consider data governance as well: the lake requires a catalog and access controls to be useful and safe.

keyIdea.text: Keep raw, diverse data in S3; use Redshift for curated, performance-sensitive analytics; query S3 from Redshift when you need both.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Warehouse vs Lake
Data Warehouse (Redshift)
Columnar MPP for structured, curated analytics
  • Purpose: Fast BI, reports, dashboards, complex SQL joins.
  • Data Shape: Modeled tables with consistent schemas.
  • Optimization: Distribution and sort keys, RA3 for managed storage.
Example
Sales and customer dimension tables loaded nightly into Redshift for dashboards and slice-and-dice queries.
Data Lake (S3)
Raw and semi-structured data at scale; flexible for many analytics engines
  • Purpose: Store raw events, logs, backups, and ML training data.
  • Data Shape: Files in Parquet/ORC/JSON; often partitioned by date or region.
  • Optimization: Partitioning and Glue Data Catalog to avoid full scans.
Example
Clickstream events stored as partitioned Parquet files, queried directly with Athena or Spectrum for exploration.
Common Mistake

Moving all raw S3 data into Redshift without partitioning or curation leads to high storage and compute costs and slow loads. Prefer Spectrum to query in place when possible.

Key Takeaway

Choose the lake for scale and flexibility; choose the warehouse for curated performance.

screens.title: Amazon Redshift Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon Redshift is a fully managed data warehouse service engineered for analytical workloads at scale. It achieves high performance through three core techniques: columnar storage, data compression, and massively parallel processing. Columnar storage stores each column together, which reduces input and output for queries that touch a subset of columns. Compression further reduces storage and scan costs, and MPP divides work across compute nodes so large joins and aggregates execute in parallel. Together these features make Redshift ideal for dashboards, BI, and complex S Q L analytics over curated data sets. A practical example: a sales analytics query that aggregates daily revenue by product category touches a few numeric and categorical columns. Because data is columnar and compressed, Redshift reads far less data than a row-based system, speeding the query and lowering input and output. A common misconception is that Redshift behaves like a transactional database; it does not. Transactional workloads with many small writes and low-latency single-row operations are better suited to OLTP databases. In Redshift, plan distribution styles and sort keys based on actual query patterns. Always profile your queries before picking keys, and remember RA3 changes the storage calculus by allowing storage to scale independently from compute.

keyIdea.title: Redshift is for analytics
keyIdea.text: Columnar storage, compression, and MPP make Redshift suitable for large-scale aggregations and joins over curated datasets.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Redshift Fundamentals
Why Redshift is fast
Columnar storage, compression, and MPP
Columnar storage
Reads only the columns needed by a query to reduce I/O for wide tables.
Compression
Reduces disk usage and speeds scans. Choose encodings based on column types.
Massively parallel processing
Distributes query work across nodes for faster joins and aggregations.
Concrete example
A daily revenue aggregation reads only date, product_id, and revenue columns. Columnar storage and compression reduce scanned bytes, and MPP aggregates across slices concurrently.
Misconception

Redshift is not designed for transactional, single-row OLTP workloads. Treat it as a specialized analytical engine.

Key Takeaway

Leverage columnar storage and MPP to minimize I/O and parallelize heavy analytical workloads.

screens.title: RA3 Instances and Managed Storage
screens.narratorSegment: RA3 instances change the storage economics of Redshift by offering managed storage that scales independently of compute. With RA3 you size the cluster for compute needs—C P U, memory, concurrency—and pay for storage based on usage. This separation prevents over-provisioning storage-heavy nodes just to gain compute. RA3 also uses a high-bandwidth cache local to compute nodes so frequently accessed data remains close, while colder blocks remain in managed storage. The result is better flexibility and often lower cost for mixed workloads with large data footprints. Consider a practical scenario: a team retains several years of historical events but runs daily aggregations that only touch recent partitions. With RA3, you keep compute modest for nightly transforms and rely on managed storage for the full dataset. A common mistake is assuming RA3 removes the need for sorting and distribution tuning—cache helps, but proper distribution keys and sort keys still matter for join and range query performance. When planning capacity, evaluate your query patterns and access skew to decide how many RA3 nodes you need for compute and how managed storage usage will impact cost.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › RA3 & Managed Storage
RA3: compute and storage decoupled
Managed storage reduces the need to size nodes for disk capacity.
Local cache
High-bandwidth cache on compute nodes keeps hot data close for low-latency access.
Managed storage
Colder data is stored separately and charged by usage.
Cost model
Compute sized for query needs; storage billed separately for capacity-efficient economics.
Best practice
Combine RA3 with targeted distribution and sort keys to maximize cache hits and query speed.
Scenario
Several years of historical telemetry are stored, but nightly transforms and recent queries only touch recent partitions. RA3 reduces the need to over-provision compute for storage needs.
Key Takeaway

Use RA3 to decouple storage growth from compute sizing, but continue to tune distribution and sort keys.

Common Mistake

Assuming RA3 eliminates the need for good data layout. Cache helps, but join and sort strategy still drives performance.

screens.title: Distribution Styles in Redshift
screens.narratorSegment: Distribution styles determine how Redshift places rows across compute slices, and they have a direct impact on join performance. AUTO lets Redshift pick a distribution based on table size and query patterns. KEY distribution places rows sharing the same key value on the same slice, minimizing data movement for joins on that key. ALL distribution copies a small dimension table to every node to avoid shuffles when joining with a large fact table. EVEN spreads rows uniformly and is a safe default for tables that are not commonly joined. A concrete example: imagine a large clicks table joined with a users table on user_id. If clicks is KEY distributed on user_id, rows with the same user_id are colocated, so the join happens locally on each slice without network-intensive redistribution. A common misconception is to use ALL for any small table; while ALL reduces shuffles, copying a table that grows can create storage overhead and maintenance complexity. Use ALL only for small dimension tables that are stable. To decide whether to use KEY, analyze your most frequent joins and choose a key that balances even data distribution and co-location. If you see skew or hot slices, reconsider your distribution key or use EVEN to avoid overload.

keyIdea.title: Place data where joins happen
keyIdea.text: Pick distribution styles based on join patterns: KEY for colocated joins, ALL for small dimensions, EVEN when no common join exists.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Distribution Styles
Distribution styles explained
AUTO — Let Redshift pick; good starting point for many tables.
KEY — Colocate rows with same key; great for frequent joins on that key.
ALL — Copy small tables to every node; avoids shuffles for stable dimensions.
EVEN — Uniform distribution; use when joins are rare or key would skew.
Example
A clicks table joined on user_id benefits from KEY distribution on user_id to reduce data movement during joins with users.
Decision flow
  1. Identify frequent join columns and table sizes.
  2. If a large table is frequently joined on a stable key, consider KEY distribution.
  3. If a small table is often joined, use ALL to avoid shuffles.
  4. If no good key exists, or to avoid skew, use EVEN or AUTO.
Pitfall

Choosing a KEY that causes data skew concentrates load on a few slices and slows queries. Analyze distribution of key values before applying KEY distribution.

screens.title: Sort Keys and Query Performance
screens.narratorSegment: Sort keys define the physical order of rows in Redshift slices and can drastically speed range-restricted queries. A compound sort key maintains columns in a specific, hierarchical order and is efficient when queries use a left-based prefix of the key. Interleaved sort keys give equal weight to multiple columns, which is helpful when your query patterns filter variably across several columns rather than a single leading column. For example, if most queries filter by date, make date the leading sort key so range scans locate relevant data blocks quickly. Alternatively, if you often filter by customer_id and product_id in different queries, consider interleaved keys so both filters benefit. Be aware of a common misconception: interleaved keys improve read performance but increase maintenance cost on large batch writes and can be more expensive during vacuum and analyze operations. Choose a sort key strategy based on dominant query shapes and the trade-off between read performance and write complexity. Always monitor query plans and distribution of filtered values to validate that the sort keys are providing expected benefits. Sort Keys and Query Performance means use compound keys for predictable left-prefix queries and interleaved keys when multiple columns are filtered in varied ways.. In practical terms, how compound and interleaved keys speed range queries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Sort Keys
Compound sort key
Best when queries filter on a predictable leading column sequence.
If most queries filter by date and then product, a compound key on (date, product) allows efficient range scans for dates, then smaller product scans within those ranges.
Interleaved sort key
Gives equal importance to multiple columns when query filters vary.
Use interleaved keys when queries filter by different columns at different times, such as customer_id in some reports and product_id in others.
Trade-off

Interleaved keys improve selective reads for multiple columns but can increase maintenance on writes. Choose based on query mix and write frequency.

Key Takeaway

Match sort key strategy to dominant query filters and monitor to confirm benefits.

screens.title: Concurrency Scaling
screens.narratorSegment: Concurrency Scaling provides temporary additional Redshift capacity to handle spikes in concurrent read queries. When your base cluster becomes saturated with read-heavy workloads—like many analysts running ad-hoc reports—Concurrency Scaling spins up transient clusters to serve queries, maintaining performance without forcing you to permanently size for peak concurrency. AWS provides a limited amount of free concurrency scaling credits each day, which can be sufficient for common burst patterns, but you should understand how your workload uses credits to avoid surprises. A concrete example: on Monday mornings the analytics team runs many dashboards and report queries simultaneously. Instead of permanently increasing your cluster to handle this peak, enable Concurrency Scaling so the extra queries are routed to transient compute. A common misconception is to think Concurrency Scaling accelerates long-running writes; it does not. It targets read queries. Also, not every query benefits equally—short, small queries gain the most. Monitor credit consumption and query latency during peak windows to tune which workloads should be offloaded or scheduled. Remember to keep the base cluster sized to handle steady-state analytic workloads, and use Concurrency Scaling to smooth bursts.

keyIdea.title: Smooth peaks with temporary capacity
keyIdea.text: Concurrency Scaling maintains read performance during spikes without permanently increasing cluster size; monitor credits and workload shape.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Concurrency Scaling
How Concurrency Scaling helps
Temporary capacity for read-heavy bursts
When to use
  • High concurrency of read queries during business hours.
  • Ad-hoc analyst workloads causing queueing.
What it does
Automatically adds transient compute to serve read queries and returns to baseline when the burst subsides.
Limits & monitoring
You receive daily free credits; monitor credit consumption and latency to avoid unexpected costs.
Misconception
It is not intended to speed long-running writes or ETL; it targets concurrent read queries only.
Key Takeaway

Use Concurrency Scaling to absorb read spikes and maintain consistent performance; track credit use and workload fit.

screens.title: Redshift Spectrum and Glue Integration
screens.narratorSegment: Redshift Spectrum lets you query data stored in S3 using S Q L without loading the data into Redshift. Spectrum relies on a metadata layer—the AWS Glue Data Catalog—to map S3 files to tables and schemas. Practically, you run a Glue Crawler to infer schema and populate the catalog, then create an external schema in Redshift that points to the Glue database. After that, you can run standard S Q L that joins internal Redshift tables with external tables stored as Parquet or ORC on S3. Concrete example: after crawling a partitioned clickstream bucket, create an external schema in Redshift that references the Glue database and an IAM role with S3 and Glue permissions. Then run a JOIN between a Redshift sales table and the Spectrum clickstream table to combine recent sales with event-level behavior. A common misconception is that Spectrum performs identically to native Redshift tables; querying external files may be slower depending on file formats and partitioning, so apply partitioning and columnar formats like Parquet to reduce scanned data. keyIdea.title: Query S3 in place
keyIdea.text: Use Glue to catalog S3 data and create an external schema in Redshift so you can join external tables with internal tables using standard SQL.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Redshift Spectrum
Code pattern: create external schema
Use an IAM role that has access to S3 and the Glue Data Catalog, then create the external schema once the catalog is populated by a crawler.
-- Create an external schema in Redshift
CREATE EXTERNAL SCHEMA clickstream_spectrum
FROM DATA CATALOG
DATABASE 'clickstream_db'
IAM_ROLE '<YOUR_REDSHIFT_IAM_ROLE_ARN>'
CREATE EXTERNAL DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS;

-- Verify the external table
SELECT * FROM clickstream_spectrum.clicks LIMIT 10;

-- Example join with an internal Redshift table
SELECT s.user_id, s.sale_date, c.page_url, c.event_time
FROM sales s
JOIN clickstream_spectrum.clicks c ON s.user_id = c.user_id
WHERE s.sale_date = '2023-01-01' AND c.event_time >= '2023-01-01T00:00:00Z'
LIMIT 10;
Practical notes
  • Use Parquet or ORC for smaller scans and faster reads.
  • Partition S3 by common filters like year/month to avoid full scans.
  • Verify Glue table schemas before querying from Redshift.
Key Takeaway

Spectrum gives you the flexibility to query S3 in place, but plan formats and partitions to control performance and cost.

screens.title: Designing an S3 Data Lake
screens.narratorSegment: A well-designed S3 data lake starts with a predictable organization and sensible partitioning. Use a hierarchical key structure that reflects common query filters, for example year=2023/month=01/day=01, so analytics engines can prune partitions and avoid scanning irrelevant data. Choose columnar storage formats like Parquet or ORC for analytical workloads because they store columns together and compress efficiently, further reducing the amount of data scanned. Also, think about lifecycle: move older raw data to cheaper storage classes or archive it if infrequent access justifies it. A concrete example: store daily clickstream events under s3://my-clickstream-data/year=2023/month=01/day=01/clicks. parquet. When users query a single day or month, Athena or Spectrum scans only the matching partitions. A common mistake is treating S3 as a flat file share without schema or partitions; this leads to full-bucket scans and high cost. Pair partitioning with Glue Crawlers to maintain an accurate Data Catalog and ensure that downstream queries see a consistent schema. Lastly, always encrypt data at rest and enforce least-privilege access through Lake Formation or IAM policies to keep the lake secure. Designing an S3 Data Lake means partition s3 by common filters and use columnar formats to minimize scan volume and improve query latency.. In practical terms, organization, partitioning, and storage formats that matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › S3 Data Lake Design
Organize using logical prefixes
Use folders that match common queries: year, month, day, region, etc.
Example prefix: s3://my-clickstream-data/year=2023/month=01/day=01/clicks.parquet. This structure enables partition pruning by query engines.
Format choice
Prefer Parquet or ORC for analytics because they are columnar and compress efficiently.
Lifecycle & security
Apply lifecycle policies to move cold data to cheaper classes and always encrypt at rest and in transit.
Pitfall

A flat unpartitioned bucket causes full scans and high query cost. Partition by typical query filters to avoid that.

Key Takeaway

Logical organization and columnar formats are the fastest, most cost-effective design for S3 analytics.

screens.title: AWS Glue Data Catalog, Crawlers, and ETL
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Glue provides the metadata and ETL capabilities that make a data lake useful. The Glue Data Catalog stores table definitions, schemas, and locations for datasets across S3 and other stores. Glue Crawlers scan your S3 prefixes, infer schemas, and populate the catalog so Athena, EMR, and Redshift Spectrum can discover and query the data. For transformation, Glue ETL jobs—written in Python or Scala—let you clean, transform, and convert data into columnar formats or curated tables. A concrete workflow: upload partitioned Parquet files to your clickstream bucket, create a Glue crawler that targets the year=2023 prefix, run the crawler to populate clickstream_db in the Glue Data Catalog, then inspect and adjust types if needed. After the catalog is accurate you can create an external schema in Redshift pointing to clickstream_db. A frequent misconception is relying solely on automatic schema inference; crawlers are a great starting point, but you should verify and, if necessary, refine schemas and partition definitions before running production queries. Glue ETL can then be used to convert raw files into optimized Parquet with partitioning conventions enforced. AWS Glue Data Catalog, Crawlers, and ETL means glue crawlers discover schemas and the data catalog makes s3 datasets queryable; glue etl prepares and converts raw data for analytics.. In practical terms, make s3 data discoverable and prepare it for analytics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Glue Catalog & ETL
Glue Data Catalog & Crawlers
Crawlers infer schema from S3 and populate the Catalog for discoverability.
Verify crawled schemas, adjust column types if needed, and ensure partitions are recognized properly before querying from Athena or Spectrum.
# Example: create a Glue crawler (CLI pattern)
aws glue create-crawler \
  --name clickstream-data-crawler \
  --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/GlueServiceRole \
  --database-name clickstream_db \
  --targets '{"S3Targets":[{"Path":"s3://<YOUR_CLICKSTREAM_BUCKET>/year=2023/"}]}' \
  --schedule "cron(0 0 * * ? *)"

# Then start the crawler
aws glue start-crawler --name clickstream-data-crawler
Glue ETL
Use Glue ETL jobs to convert, clean, and partition data into Parquet for efficient analytics.
Practical Tip

Run crawlers after ingest, then use ETL jobs to standardize formats and push curated data into sinks or partitioned folders.

screens.title: Lake Formation: Centralized Security and Governance
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Lake Formation builds a centralized security layer on top of the Glue Data Catalog and S3. Instead of scattering S3 bucket policies and IAM rules, Lake Formation lets you register S3 locations and define permissions at the database, table, column, or even row level. These permissions are then enforced by integrated services such as Athena, EMR, and Redshift Spectrum, simplifying compliance and minimizing accidental over-privilege. Lake Formation also supports fine-grained row-level filtering and column masking, which is essential when different teams require access to different slices of the same table. A concrete scenario: the marketing team needs access to customer demographics but cannot see financial columns like payment details. In Lake Formation you grant SELECT on specific columns to the marketing role while restricting sensitive columns. Another common mistake is to leave S3 objects open or to grant broad S3 read permissions and assume analytics services will enforce controls. With Lake Formation, you can remove direct S3 access from analyst roles and force all analytics queries through the centralized policy engine. Always register buckets with Lake Formation and design least-privilege permissions for service roles and analyst roles.

Govern with Lake Formation
Centralized, fine-grained access control for data lakes
Capabilities
  • Table, column, and row-level permissions.

Grant marketing role SELECT on demographic columns but deny access to financial columns. Remove direct S3 access to force queries through Lake Formation policies.
Pitfall

Relying solely on IAM and S3 policies for fine-grained analytics access becomes unmanageable at scale. Centralize permissions in Lake Formation instead.

Key Takeaway

Use Lake Formation to reduce policy sprawl and enforce least-privilege access across analytics services.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll explore two complementary pillars of analytics on AWS: a high-performance data warehouse using Amazon Redshift, and a scalable data lake built on Amazon S3. You will learn how Redshift uses columnar storage, compression, and massively parallel processing to run complex analytics, and how RA3 instances separate compute and managed storage so you can scale each independently. You'll also see how Redshift Spectrum queries open formats in S3 using the AWS Glue Data Catalog, making a lakehouse-style architecture possible. On the data lake side, we'll cover practical S3 design: logical organization, partitioning by common filters like year and month, and why those choices reduce query cost. Then we'll examine Glue as the metadata and ETL backbone, and Lake Formation as the centralized security layer for table, column, and row permissions. Through a short hands-on workflow you will configure a crawler, create an external schema, and write a cross-source S Q L join. By the end you will know when to keep data in place on S3 and query it from Redshift, and when to load curated data into Redshift. We'll emphasize common mistakes—like missing partitioning or ignoring distribution keys—and practical mitigations. Ready to begin designing a balanced, cost-effective analytics platform?

Over the next fifteen minutes you'll gain concrete skills for designing and operating analytics platforms. First, you'll learn to design scalable and cost-effective Redshift warehouses: choose instance types, employ RA3 managed storage, and select distribution and sort keys based on query patterns. For example, when joins repeatedly use a customer_id, a KEY distribution can dramatically reduce data movement. Second, you'll implement advanced Redshift features like Concurrency Scaling and Spectrum so your cluster handles concurrent read bursts and queries S3 in place. We'll show how Spectrum leverages the Glue Data Catalog so you can query Parquet files without loading them. These objectives matter because analytics at petabyte scale needs predictable performance and cost control. You'll practice reasoning about compute versus storage, and how to avoid common mistakes like uniform sort keys for all queries. Each objective ties directly to a hands-on workflow: crawling S3 with Glue, creating an external schema in Redshift, and writing a cross-source S Q L join. By the end you will be able to choose when to keep data in S3 and when to load it into Redshift, and you'll know the tools for controlling access and metadata.

This second objectives slide ties the learning goals to a concrete workflow you'll practice. First, design: pick RA3 or other instance families and pick distribution or sort keys by analyzing query patterns and join columns. For example, a KEY distribution on user_id reduces data movement when joining large event and user tables. Second, operate: enable Concurrency Scaling to absorb spikes in ad-hoc BI queries and understand the daily credits model so you budget query bursts wisely. Third, integrate: build a data lake on S3 with partitioned Parquet files, use a Glue Crawler to populate the Data Catalog, and verify schema correctness before querying. Finally, secure and manage: register S3 with Lake Formation, grant table- or column-level SELECT permissions to roles, and avoid direct S3 access so queries go through the centralized enforcement layer. The hands-on task follows these steps: create a bucket, upload partitioned Parquet, run a crawler, create an external schema in Redshift, and write a S Q L join between Redshift and Spectrum tables. This maps objectives to repeatable steps and prepares you to design both an efficient pipeline and a secure governance model.

Understanding the practical difference between a data warehouse and a data lake is the foundation of good analytics architecture. A data warehouse like Redshift is optimized for structured, curated datasets and complex S Q L analytics. It uses columnar storage and MPP to accelerate aggregations and joins over large curated tables. A data lake on S3 is a flexible store for raw and semi-structured data at any scale; it's ideal for long-term retention, exploration, and machine learning. A simple rule of thumb: put long-term raw events, logs, and historical snapshots in the lake; keep curated, modeled tables that power dashboards in the warehouse. A concrete example: clickstream events arriving daily are best landed in S3 as partitioned Parquet files. Analysts can explore patterns in-place using Athena or Spectrum. When you need consistent, highly tuned reports that join sales and customer dimensions nightly, load those curated results into Redshift for fast BI queries. A common misconception is thinking one must always move everything into Redshift. That approach can be expensive and slow at petabyte scale. Instead, query S3 in place with Spectrum when possible, and load only the curated subsets that need warehouse performance. Consider data governance as well: the lake requires a catalog and access controls to be useful and safe.

Amazon Redshift is a fully managed data warehouse service engineered for analytical workloads at scale. It achieves high performance through three core techniques: columnar storage, data compression, and massively parallel processing. Columnar storage stores each column together, which reduces input and output for queries that touch a subset of columns. Compression further reduces storage and scan costs, and MPP divides work across compute nodes so large joins and aggregates execute in parallel. Together these features make Redshift ideal for dashboards, BI, and complex S Q L analytics over curated data sets. A practical example: a sales analytics query that aggregates daily revenue by product category touches a few numeric and categorical columns. Because data is columnar and compressed, Redshift reads far less data than a row-based system, speeding the query and lowering input and output. A common misconception is that Redshift behaves like a transactional database; it does not. Transactional workloads with many small writes and low-latency single-row operations are better suited to OLTP databases. In Redshift, plan distribution styles and sort keys based on actual query patterns. Always profile your queries before picking keys, and remember RA3 changes the storage calculus by allowing storage to scale independently from compute.

RA3 instances change the storage economics of Redshift by offering managed storage that scales independently of compute. With RA3 you size the cluster for compute needs—C P U, memory, concurrency—and pay for storage based on usage. This separation prevents over-provisioning storage-heavy nodes just to gain compute. RA3 also uses a high-bandwidth cache local to compute nodes so frequently accessed data remains close, while colder blocks remain in managed storage. The result is better flexibility and often lower cost for mixed workloads with large data footprints. Consider a practical scenario: a team retains several years of historical events but runs daily aggregations that only touch recent partitions. With RA3, you keep compute modest for nightly transforms and rely on managed storage for the full dataset. A common mistake is assuming RA3 removes the need for sorting and distribution tuning—cache helps, but proper distribution keys and sort keys still matter for join and range query performance. When planning capacity, evaluate your query patterns and access skew to decide how many RA3 nodes you need for compute and how managed storage usage will impact cost.

Distribution styles determine how Redshift places rows across compute slices, and they have a direct impact on join performance. AUTO lets Redshift pick a distribution based on table size and query patterns. KEY distribution places rows sharing the same key value on the same slice, minimizing data movement for joins on that key. ALL distribution copies a small dimension table to every node to avoid shuffles when joining with a large fact table. EVEN spreads rows uniformly and is a safe default for tables that are not commonly joined. A concrete example: imagine a large clicks table joined with a users table on user_id. If clicks is KEY distributed on user_id, rows with the same user_id are colocated, so the join happens locally on each slice without network-intensive redistribution. A common misconception is to use ALL for any small table; while ALL reduces shuffles, copying a table that grows can create storage overhead and maintenance complexity. Use ALL only for small dimension tables that are stable. To decide whether to use KEY, analyze your most frequent joins and choose a key that balances even data distribution and co-location. If you see skew or hot slices, reconsider your distribution key or use EVEN to avoid overload.

Sort keys define the physical order of rows in Redshift slices and can drastically speed range-restricted queries. A compound sort key maintains columns in a specific, hierarchical order and is efficient when queries use a left-based prefix of the key. Interleaved sort keys give equal weight to multiple columns, which is helpful when your query patterns filter variably across several columns rather than a single leading column. For example, if most queries filter by date, make date the leading sort key so range scans locate relevant data blocks quickly. Alternatively, if you often filter by customer_id and product_id in different queries, consider interleaved keys so both filters benefit. Be aware of a common misconception: interleaved keys improve read performance but increase maintenance cost on large batch writes and can be more expensive during vacuum and analyze operations. Choose a sort key strategy based on dominant query shapes and the trade-off between read performance and write complexity. Always monitor query plans and distribution of filtered values to validate that the sort keys are providing expected benefits. Sort Keys and Query Performance means use compound keys for predictable left-prefix queries and interleaved keys when multiple columns are filtered in varied ways.. In practical terms, how compound and interleaved keys speed range queries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Concurrency Scaling provides temporary additional Redshift capacity to handle spikes in concurrent read queries. When your base cluster becomes saturated with read-heavy workloads—like many analysts running ad-hoc reports—Concurrency Scaling spins up transient clusters to serve queries, maintaining performance without forcing you to permanently size for peak concurrency. AWS provides a limited amount of free concurrency scaling credits each day, which can be sufficient for common burst patterns, but you should understand how your workload uses credits to avoid surprises. A concrete example: on Monday mornings the analytics team runs many dashboards and report queries simultaneously. Instead of permanently increasing your cluster to handle this peak, enable Concurrency Scaling so the extra queries are routed to transient compute. A common misconception is to think Concurrency Scaling accelerates long-running writes; it does not. It targets read queries. Also, not every query benefits equally—short, small queries gain the most. Monitor credit consumption and query latency during peak windows to tune which workloads should be offloaded or scheduled. Remember to keep the base cluster sized to handle steady-state analytic workloads, and use Concurrency Scaling to smooth bursts.

Redshift Spectrum lets you query data stored in S3 using S Q L without loading the data into Redshift. Spectrum relies on a metadata layer—the AWS Glue Data Catalog—to map S3 files to tables and schemas. Practically, you run a Glue Crawler to infer schema and populate the catalog, then create an external schema in Redshift that points to the Glue database. After that, you can run standard S Q L that joins internal Redshift tables with external tables stored as Parquet or ORC on S3. Concrete example: after crawling a partitioned clickstream bucket, create an external schema in Redshift that references the Glue database and an IAM role with S3 and Glue permissions. Then run a JOIN between a Redshift sales table and the Spectrum clickstream table to combine recent sales with event-level behavior. A common misconception is that Spectrum performs identically to native Redshift tables; querying external files may be slower depending on file formats and partitioning, so apply partitioning and columnar formats like Parquet to reduce scanned data. Below is the S Q L pattern to create an external schema and verify the external table, which you'll use in the hands-on task.

A well-designed S3 data lake starts with a predictable organization and sensible partitioning. Use a hierarchical key structure that reflects common query filters, for example year=2023/month=01/day=01, so analytics engines can prune partitions and avoid scanning irrelevant data. Choose columnar storage formats like Parquet or ORC for analytical workloads because they store columns together and compress efficiently, further reducing the amount of data scanned. Also, think about lifecycle: move older raw data to cheaper storage classes or archive it if infrequent access justifies it. A concrete example: store daily clickstream events under s3://my-clickstream-data/year=2023/month=01/day=01/clicks. parquet. When users query a single day or month, Athena or Spectrum scans only the matching partitions. A common mistake is treating S3 as a flat file share without schema or partitions; this leads to full-bucket scans and high cost. Pair partitioning with Glue Crawlers to maintain an accurate Data Catalog and ensure that downstream queries see a consistent schema. Lastly, always encrypt data at rest and enforce least-privilege access through Lake Formation or IAM policies to keep the lake secure. AWS Glue provides the metadata and ETL capabilities that make a data lake useful. The Glue Data Catalog stores table definitions, schemas, and locations for datasets across S3 and other stores. Glue Crawlers scan your S3 prefixes, infer schemas, and populate the catalog so Athena, EMR, and Redshift Spectrum can discover and query the data. For transformation, Glue ETL jobs—written in Python or Scala—let you clean, transform, and convert data into columnar formats or curated tables. A concrete workflow: upload partitioned Parquet files to your clickstream bucket, create a Glue crawler that targets the year=2023 prefix, run the crawler to populate clickstream_db in the Glue Data Catalog, then inspect and adjust types if needed. After the catalog is accurate you can create an external schema in Redshift pointing to clickstream_db. A frequent misconception is relying solely on automatic schema inference; crawlers are a great starting point, but you should verify and, if necessary, refine schemas and partition definitions before running production queries. Glue ETL can then be used to convert raw files into optimized Parquet with partitioning conventions enforced. AWS Lake Formation builds a centralized security layer on top of the Glue Data Catalog and S3. Instead of scattering S3 bucket policies and IAM rules, Lake Formation lets you register S3 locations and define permissions at the database, table, column, or even row level. These permissions are then enforced by integrated services such as Athena, EMR, and Redshift Spectrum, simplifying compliance and minimizing accidental over-privilege. Lake Formation also supports fine-grained row-level filtering and column masking, which is essential when different teams require access to different slices of the same table. A concrete scenario: the marketing team needs access to customer demographics but cannot see financial columns like payment details. In Lake Formation you grant SELECT on specific columns to the marketing role while restricting sensitive columns. Another common mistake is to leave S3 objects open or to grant broad S3 read permissions and assume analytics services will enforce controls. With Lake Formation, you can remove direct S3 access from analyst roles and force all analytics queries through the centralized policy engine. Always register buckets with Lake Formation and design least-privilege permissions for service roles and analyst roles.

These key concepts summarize the Redshift side of the chapter. Amazon Redshift is a fully managed data warehouse optimized for analytical workloads using columnar storage and MPP. RA3 instance types provide managed storage that scales separately from compute and include a high-bandwidth cache to keep hot data nearby. Redshift Spectrum lets you query data directly in S3 using standard S Q L by leveraging the Glue Data Catalog as the metadata layer. Keep these concepts in mind when designing architectures: use Redshift for curated performance, consider RA3 for large datasets that grow, and leverage Spectrum to avoid unnecessary data movement when querying S3 data in place. Reflect: which combination of managed storage and Spectrum would let you avoid costly bulk loads while still delivering fast BI queries for recent, curated subsets of your data?

These final concepts focus on the data lake and metadata layer. A data lake on Amazon S3 stores raw and semi-structured data at scale and should be organized with logical prefixes and partitioning for efficient query pruning. The AWS Glue Data Catalog centralizes metadata for datasets and is populated by Glue Crawlers that infer schemas. Glue ETL jobs let you transform and prepare raw data into optimized columnar formats. Lake Formation acts as a centralized security control, letting you define table, column, and row-level permissions that are enforced across analytics services. Together these components make a secure, discoverable, and queryable lakehouse architecture when combined with Redshift Spectrum.
